• Common name: Swamp Dwarf Crayfish
  • Optimal tank size: about 40 litres
  • Breeding: easy
  • Optimal KH: 3–15
  • Nitrate: less than 20 ppm
  • Diet: detritivore / omnivore
  • Temperament: conditionally peaceful
  • Lifespan: up to 2 years
  • Colour forms: orange-red, light brown, grayish or even blue

Warning: NEVER release any crayfish species, including Cambarellus puer, into the wild. Many decapod crustacean species are confirmed or suspected carriers of pathogens that can cause mass mortality among native crustaceans.

Cambarellus puer is easy to care for and breeds readily. Because of their small size they do not take up much space in the tank. The only problem is that this species is fairly rare in the pet trade.

The main problem with dwarf crayfish is that they look very similar, and even professional aquarists often have a hard time telling them apart. Many of these species can also crossbreed, creating new colour morphs and patterns, so crayfish seen online are quite likely to be hybrids. General colours: Cambarellus puer – orange-red to light brown; C. ninae – brown; C. montezumae – yellow; C. patzcuarensis – orange; C. shufeldtii – grey/reddish to brown; C. texanus – olive to brown; C. diminutus – grey/reddish to brown or blue.

The blue strain is not stable and often turns brown after a molt, so ask the seller about it before buying.

Cambarellus puer occurs from southern Illinois and Missouri southward along the Mississippi River to Louisiana, and westward to southeastern Oklahoma and eastern Texas.

Its range is almost identical to that of Cambarellus shufeldtii, except that C. shufeldtii reaches further west into Texas.

Their habitat is areas near swamps, ditches, lakes, ponds and sluggish streams. Cambarellus puer prefers shallow, slow-moving, muddy habitats with dense emergent and submerged vegetation where they can dig and hide.

The minimum recommended tank size is 20 litres. Ideally a 40-litre tank suits them much better. Like most crayfish they are quite active and need plenty of room to crawl, eat and explore. Keeping stable water parameters in nano tanks can be a challenge even for experienced aquarists.

A group of 3–5 crayfish can live comfortably in a 40-litre tank if they have enough hiding places.

Tip: Cambarellus puer is a great escape artist, so use a tight-fitting lid.

Care is quite easy and straightforward. These crustaceans are not high-maintenance and adapt well to captivity.

Substrate: soil and/or sand replicates their natural environment. A depth of 7–10 cm is enough for them to construct burrows if necessary.

Decorations: shelter and protection are a key requirement for any freshwater crayfish. They need plenty of dark hiding places made of stones, driftwood, PVC pipe, plastic tunnels, plants and so on. If several are kept, or they share a community tank, every animal needs several hiding places in different parts of the tank, especially during molting.

Acclimate them properly when introducing them to the tank.

Molting: to grow, Cambarellus puer must shed its exoskeleton. Molting also allows damage to be repaired and lost appendages to be replaced. The process has phases: pre-molt, molt, post-molt and inter-molt. When a crayfish is about to molt it looks for a place to hide, otherwise it can easily fall prey to tankmates.

  • NEVER disturb a crayfish that is molting. Do not panic if you have not seen them for a few days.
  • Keep putting in and replacing food; you never know when they will emerge.
  • Keep giving calcium-rich food.
  • Do not remove the old exoskeleton; it contains lots of minerals and the crayfish will eat it later.

Temperature: ideally 20–24°C, but they easily survive a wide range of 15–30°C, so in most cases room temperature suits them.

pH: 6.5–8.0.

Hardness: KH 3–15 and GH 3–20.

Nitrate: less than 20 ppm.

Although some aquarists keep them in tap water, RO/DI water remineralised with Salty Shrimp GH/KH+ is recommended, as it allows control of water parameters and optimal conditions.

Filtration: it does not matter much and any filter will do. For small tanks sponge or matten filters are best: the crayfish will not damage them as large crayfish often do, and they are cheap, easy to maintain and clean, provide plenty of surface to graze on and are safe for baby crayfish.

Canister or hang-on-back filters suit large tanks, but the intake must be covered with a sponge if you want to breed them.

Lighting: no special requirements. Cambarellus puer is nocturnal. If you have plants, adapt the lighting to their needs.

Use a tight-fitting lid.

Cambarellus puer are opportunistic eaters and will eat about anything edible. In captivity, for best growth they need a good mix of meat and vegetation. Omnivore.

  • Shrimp pellets and granules
  • Fish food (flakes, etc.)
  • Shrimp food (crustacean foods)
  • Vegetables (broccoli, cabbage, carrot, cucumber, lettuce, corn, spinach, peas, squash, leafy greens, etc.)
  • Fruits (apple, banana, melon, mango, etc.)
  • Leaves
  • Frozen bloodworms
  • Detritus worms
  • Brine shrimp
  • Tubifex worms
  • Earthworms
  • Freshly crushed snails
  • Dead fish or shrimp, etc.

Regularly give leaves (Indian almond leaves, beech leaves, oak leaves, etc.), as they feed on these and need the detritus from the leaves.

Like all crustaceans they have an exoskeleton hardened by calcium salts, so supplement the diet with eggshells, cuttlebone, etc., and regularly feed specialised invertebrate foods to provide enough calcium.

Feeding frequency: adults 3–4 times a week, juveniles daily. Do not let them starve, or they may even cannibalise each other.

Food can be left for 24 hours before removal. Remove uneaten food, otherwise it fouls the water and causes problems (black beard algae, hydras, planaria, etc.). It is better to feed in the evening or at night because they are nocturnal. Change the diet at least every week or two rather than giving the same food all the time.

Cambarellus puer is not as aggressive as its cousin the Dwarf Mexican crayfish (Cambarellus patzcuarensis). They are considered social animals and benefit from the company of their own species, but are not completely peaceful: they have complex territorial interactions and in an overcrowded tank they may fight, thereby regulating their numbers.

They can dig in the substrate but are not obligate burrowers, which is good for planted tanks as they will not ruin the aquascape. They do not eat healthy plants and mostly use plants as hiding spots, so they can be kept in planted aquariums.

  • Social: yes
  • Active: yes
  • Peaceful: yes (generally)
  • Burrowers: no (generally)

They are probably one of the most social and peaceful crayfish, but only under several conditions: a male to female ratio of 1:3 (males in particular are likely to fight in small enclosures); lots of hiding places; and they must not be hungry, since they compete for food and become more aggressive. Following these rules cannot guarantee results, and you may need to intervene.

Fish: do not keep with aggressive, bottom-dwelling, slow-moving or long-finned fish (such as Betta). They are often kept with small peaceful fish like guppies, neon tetras, mollies, Endlers and dwarf swordtails.

Shrimp: there are many reports of them being kept in shrimp tanks without losses, but caution is advised with expensive shrimp, as shrimp can be caught, especially when molting. Keep the crayfish well fed and provide enough hiding places.

Snails: they usually do not bother big snails, but may nip off their antennae, and baby snails can become a snack.

Bad tankmates: larger or aggressive fish; bottom-dwelling, slow-moving and long-finned fish; any other crayfish species; other freshwater crabs; dwarf frogs.

Cambarellus puer is gonochoristic (each individual is either male or female). Sex can be determined externally:

  • Females are a little larger than males.
  • Female claws are shorter and thicker; males have relatively slender and long claws.
  • Males have a trilobed (Y-shaped) reproductive organ with paired pereopods. Females have seminal receptacles and lack the extra pleopods behind the walking legs; instead of a triangular arrangement of small legs there is a small nub, which indicates a female.

Mating: the male and female position their bodies face-to-face, with the male on top holding the female's claws with his own. This generally lasts a few minutes. In the wild there are two periods of reproductive activity: late winter to early spring and mid-summer. Most males do not breed in their first year. Males show no mate guarding, so females can mate with several males.

Eggs: ovigerous females carry a few dozen eggs, 1.0–1.1 mm in diameter. Hatching takes 4–5 weeks depending on temperature. Freshwater crayfish have no larval stage; what emerges is a juvenile with most of the adult appendages.

Young: after hatching, juveniles remain attached to the female's pleopods by a telson thread. Females secrete maternal pheromones that encourage the young to stay close. Young stay with the mother for the first two molts (about 7–10 days).

Rearing: some non-ovigerous females and males may eat juveniles, and the attractant effect declines over time so that females become predatory again. After hatching and separation from the mother, keep the babies in a separate tank. Feed baby dwarf crayfish daily; if well fed they are less aggressive towards each other.

Appearance: adults rarely exceed 37 mm in total length. Populations show a pigmentation polymorphism: the carapace and abdomen have either two brown to black stripes or two rows of spots running along their entire length. These two patterns are controlled by a single gene, with the striped phenotype dominant over the spotted one. The background colour of the upper and lateral sides of the carapace, abdomen and claws can be orange-red, light brown, grayish or even blue. The underside is usually white to cream. The claw tips often lack orange coloration; the claws are small and slender with short fingers.

Lifespan: about 1.5 years; under optimal conditions up to 2 years in the tank.
